working, visual journey in Barkpark Cloud

blocks.text: Acceptance — three proofs, one of them negative

content.value: Journey:
a stranger walks create → add support → see the group, unaided, in the console.
Offload:
one heavy capacity task — a full workspace export of the class the main provably cannot afford — runs on a support while the main stays responsive, visibly.
Engine:

two fence-disjoint canary cycles run concurrently and merge serially; then two deliberately OVERLAPPING fences are injected and the allocator is PROVEN to refuse them. Without the negative half, the allocator's green proves nothing.

Groups beyond 1 main + 2 supports · the Chat-agent driver (MVP-0 uses external Claude Code) · lease-lapse and resilience automation · the auto work-source (the dial ships; that position refuses until the multiplier is measured) · and ALL of commerce. Note what is NOT deferred: the visual journey and gate hardening both ride MVP-0, because the journey is the product and full-auto is the default.

blocks.title: Out of scope for MVP-0, in writing

content.value: An earlier cut of this plan recommended one box per fleet with soft-isolated members. The offload purpose kills that:
a support on the main's own box adds no capacity
— offload REQUIRES another box. So the ruling is amended, and it is simpler:

rows.value: The product, billing and cockpit unit: one main + its supports, anchored on the main
Every member is its own instance — the existing provisioning unit (site-spawner, instance lifecycle, Hetzner client). Add-support = provision + bind.
Cross-customer isolation falls out for free (separate boxes). Intra-group trust is soft — same owner, same repo — over the members' private channel.
Supports are sized per task class: a big-memory support for exports, lean ones for cycles. The main stays ≥16 GB; a support's size is a property of its job.

content.value: The crown-proof export demands 2235 MiB beside a live BEAM — impossible on the 3.8 GB main it was tried on, trivial on an 8–16 GB support that runs nothing else. Capacity classes turn a structural impossibility into a dropdown choice.
The hub-and-spoke shape makes pricing honest and incremental: the base is the
$29 dev server you already have
; the upsell unit is
the support server
. No fleet SKU, no tier table to study — you add capacity the way you add it in the console: one support at a time, priced by size class.
Sophistication lives in bounding the variable that bites. The COGS has two parts and they behave nothing alike:

rows.label: Token spend
rows.note: dominant · variable · can turn a sale into a loss

content.value: Concurrent cycles burn tokens fast, and this project's own record shows the monthly spend limit being hit
repeatedly

. Never bundle unbounded tokens into a flat price. The instruments already exist — the fleet-wide token meter is in the engine plan, and the repo carries a verified cost formula (note that cache writes are roughly 59% of agent cost).

blocks.title: The recurring failure this must not reproduce

items.label: Base
items.text: Your Personal Development Server, unchanged at its rung. The fleet is an attachment to it, never a replacement for it.

items.label: Upsell
items.text: Each support is priced like a PDS plus an orchestration premium, by size class. Adding and removing supports is elastic — a support is disposable by doctrine, so month-to-month elasticity is honest.

items.label: Tokens
items.text: Bring-your-own key, or metered pass-through with margin — always behind a HARD per-fleet cap that halts cycles, not just updates. The cap is a product feature, reusing the meter the main needs anyway.

snapshot.title: MVP-0 · Setup + offload + engine — the console journey, one real offload, canary pair, negative fence test

MVP-2 · Commerce — self-serve provisioning, billing, per-support metering

rows.value: A stranger walks the journey; a heavy task provably leaves the main; the fence allocator can actually refuse — all visual, all in the console
Four-support concurrency, the cycle-halting spend cap firing before spend runs away, and the first queued outside users running their own fleets via the pilot lane
A fleet grows from the console for someone who is not you — metered per support and billable

items.value: Is 1 main + 4 supports the shape the marketing leads with, or is capacity-by-class (one big export support + N cycle supports) the honest headline?
Uniform supports, or task-class sizing (export-class, cycle-class) from day one? Class sizing is more honest to the offload story but adds a choice to the add-support flow.
BYO key or metered pass-through as the default? BYO bounds risk to near zero; metered captures more revenue but carries spend exposure.
Should the group be a first-class noun (bp fleet ...) or a label that scopes existing bp cloud verbs? The label is cheaper and keeps the design law; the noun reads better.
The twin doctrine says a free local fleet must be possible — how many supports does one local machine honestly sustain before the box is the limit?

content.value: File the Personal Dev Fleet epic and cut the MVP-0 tasks: the group object, the add-support console flow, the dispatcher with capacity routing, the fence allocator, the merge arbiter, the offload proof, and the positive-plus-negative fence acceptance. Then the fleet starts building itself, through
bp-epic-cycle
— the same way it will build everything else.

BARKPARK CLOUD · PRODUCT + MVP PLAN

Personal Dev Fleet

Barkpark Cloud · MVP plan · Rev 3 · 2026-07-21

Start with your dev server. Add support servers to it — and the group becomes a fleet. The supports exist to serve the main: they take capacity work off it — heavy exports, builds, concurrent epic cycles — while the main stays your fast, responsive home. Set up visually in Barkpark Cloud, at flagship grade, from the first click.

You don't buy a fleet. Your dev server grows one — one support at a time.

1
Dev server — the main
+N
Supports, one click each
2
Fleet dials (autonomy · source)
3

70%

The export that proves offload
  1. 1. The ladder
  2. 2. The shape: one main, N supports
  3. 3. A support IS a Personal Development Server
  4. 4. Three layers: engine, cockpit, commerce
  5. 5. The setup experience is the MVP
  6. 6. The cockpit is not a later phase
  7. 7. The two dials
  8. 8. MVP-0 — setup, offload, engine
  9. 9. The infrastructure unit
  10. 10. Pricing
  11. 11. The sequence
  12. 12. Open questions

The ladder

RungWhat you getPrice
Personal Localbin/barkpark up — works offline, free foreverFree
Personal Development ServerOne personal cloud twin; scrubbed pulls from real data; reset and re-hydrate fearlessly$29 / mo
Personal Dev FleetYour dev server plus N support servers that exist to serve it — capacity offload and concurrent epic cyclesPer support server
The twin doctrine is inherited, not renegotiated
Paid buys convenience, never capability. A fleet must remain buildable locally for free — the cloud tier sells the boxes, the provisioning, and the orchestration, not the ability. And the ladder is now literally additive: the fleet is not a separate product, it is the $29 rung growing.

The shape: one main, N supports

The fleet is a hub and its spokes. The main is your dev server — it keeps the brain: the task ledger, Chat, Studio, your data. Support servers are subordinate by design: runners that claim capacity tasks from the main's ledger, do the heavy work, and report back. Nothing lives on a support that anyone would miss.

What a capacity task is

Heavy exports
The proof is in this repo's own history: the PDS crown proof waited ELEVEN WAVES because a 2.2 GB workspace export could not fit beside the live API on a 3.8 GB box. A support server is exactly the box that job needed.
Epic-cycle waves
A bp-epic-cycle wave — worktree, builders, gates — runs on a support while the main stays interactive. N supports = N concurrent waves, under fence control.
Builds, indexing, batch
Site builds (the measured cond_b contention channel), search reindexing, media rendition sweeps, migration rehearsal — anything the main is too busy or too small for.
The asymmetry is the safety
The main never runs capacity work; a support never holds state worth keeping. A support that dies or drifts is deleted and re-provisioned — disposability is inherited straight from the PDS doctrine. That is why offload can default to aggressive.

A support IS a Personal Development Server

This is not branding — it collapses a whole category of work. PDS's shipped data plane is the fleet's support provisioning mechanism:

ProvisionScrubbed pull A new support hydrates from the main through the dev-profile export — deny-by-default, fail-closed, provably zero secrets.
RecycleReset fearlessly Between tasks a support resets and re-pulls rather than accumulating drift. Disposability is the point of a PDS and exactly what a capacity runner needs.
ConvergeMerge-import By-id upsert reconciliation means a re-pull is a refresh, not a rebuild.
Supports need no Barkpark of their own
Because the ledger is central on the main, a support is just a runner — a Claude Code process plus its worktrees, with bp pointed at the main. Only the main needs a full Barkpark with Chat. That keeps a support cheap to add, cheap to size up, and trivial to throw away.

Three layers: engine, cockpit, commerce

You cannot debug — let alone trust — a fleet you cannot enter and observe. Entry and ergonomics are foundational; billing is not. And in this product the cockpit is not even a layer OVER the product — the visual setup experience IS the product's first act.

Engine — MVP-0
Fence allocator, merge arbiter, dispatcher, capacity offload, concurrent cycles in isolated worktrees. Single-tenant. The thing that must hold or there is no product.
Cockpit — MVP-0
The visual Cloud console journey plus bp cloud and the herd. Needed on day one by every operator — and it IS the product's headline feature, not supporting infrastructure.
Commerce — later
Billing and tier enforcement for strangers — deferrable. But a PILOT LANE is not: early users are already queued, and they get fleets (manual provisioning, BYO keys) before a storefront exists.

The setup experience is the MVP

The MVP is not a daemon with a README — it is a working, visual journey in Barkpark Cloud. The operator console the GUI-remake epic shipped is the stage; this feature is what it exists to show off. Four moments, each one visible:

  1. Create your dev server

    The existing PDS flow in the Cloud console — provision, verify, enter. Nothing new to learn: the fleet's main is just your dev server, and it is the main from birth.

  2. Add a support server

    One action on the dev server's own card: Add support. It provisions a runner, binds it to the main, pulls a scrubbed dataset, and joins the group. No separate fleet product, no form pages — the group exists the moment the first support does.

  3. See the group become a fleet

    The fleet card: the main with its supports around it, live status pills (working, blocked, idle), the capacity queue, the merge queue, spend so far. One glance answers: what is my fleet doing right now?

  4. Offload — and feel the main stay fast

    Route a heavy task — a full export, an epic-cycle wave — to the fleet. Watch it leave the main, run on a support, and land back as a merged PR or a finished artifact, while the main never stutters. That felt difference is the demo.

This journey IS the acceptance test
MVP-0 is not done when the daemons work — it is done when a stranger can walk these four steps unaided, in the console, and feel the offload. The flagship bar applies to every click: if a flow is not effortless, it is not done.

The cockpit is not a later phase

The requirement is plain: enter these clouds easily, and make the fleet convenient to work with. The console journey above is the primary surface; the terminal cockpit mirrors it — and most of that mirror already ships. The fleet does not need a new console, it needs the existing surfaces, scoped to a group.

The bar is flagship, not founder-tolerance
This is built founder-first but it is for many people, and people are already waiting to try it. Efficiency and ease of interaction are not polish — they are the product's most important feature and the demonstration of what Barkpark can do. Nothing ships at works-for-me quality; if a flow is not effortless for a stranger, it is not done.
What you needAlready shipped
See the fleetbp cloud status — every Barkpark ranked, bucketed: attention · in-flight · healthy
Watch the agentsbp chat — lands on “the herd”: agent-state pills, sorted blocked-first
Enter an instancebp cloud open instance <name> deep link · Studio tmux console, admin-gated
Auth once, reach allbp login device-link + bp instance credentials <id> — the minted admin token, no SSH
Switch contextbp use / bp servers — named, known, active
Meter spendbp cloud usage — honest counts, never a fake zero
Fleet-wide brakebp cloud rollout halt
Provision · ship · gatebp cloud instance create · bp cloud deploy · bp cloud verify
Cycle ledgerbp cycle — already one project-scoped authority for local AND cloud agents
The design law that follows
Do not build a new control surface — extend the console, bp cloud and the herd. A Personal Dev Fleet that requires its own bespoke console has already failed the convenience test it exists to pass. Visual first, CLI parity always.

The five genuine gaps

Gap 1No group object Instances are a flat list. Nothing says these ARE one group anchored on a main — so status, open, usage and rollout cannot scope to a fleet, and the console cannot draw the fleet card.
Gap 2No fleet context bp use is per-server; there is no group context unit and no way to address a member by ROLE — main, support-2. This is PDS gap G5, still open.
Gap 3No cycle brake bp cloud rollout halt brakes autoupdates, not WORK. A fleet-scoped spend cap that halts running cycles does not exist yet — and it is the guardrail the pricing model depends on.
Gap 4Herd is chat-only The herd shows chat sessions with agent-state pills. A fleet operator also needs capacity tasks, cycles, claims, fences and the merge queue in that same attention-sorted view.
Gap 5Console not fleet-reachable The Studio tmux console exists and is admin-gated by default, but is not reachable per-support FROM the fleet card — which is exactly the enter-easily path.
What this buys
Closing five gaps against surfaces that already rank, open, authenticate, meter and brake is a fraction of building a fleet console from scratch — and it means the fleet is operable from the first support it ever gains.

The two dials

A hostile review of this plan surfaced three fate questions — who may advance main, who authors the work, who is the first customer. The answers came back with one shape: the two decisions that determine what this product IS are not policies to fix — they are fleet-level dials, surfaced in the cockpit, switchable per fleet.

Dial 1 — Autonomy
full · tiered · manual. FULL is the default: the fleet merges on green and you sample afterward. Tiered by choice: auto-merge on low-risk fences, human approval on core paths — the fence map doubles as the trust map. Manual caps throughput at your attention.
Dial 2 — Work source
backlog · wish · auto. Backlog drains the existing ready-task pool. Wish: you write high-level wishes and the main runs strategize-then-decide to cut and fence the roster. Auto: the fleet generates its own strategy — the biggest agent risk, sequenced last.
Full-auto by default makes the gate the safety case
If the default is merge-on-green with no human in the loop, the green must be one a broken build could NOT also produce. Gate hardening stops being hygiene and becomes the product's core safety property: protective tests, mutation-proven guards, and an arbiter that refuses advisory-red merges. This joins MVP-0's acceptance, not its backlog.
The dials land in order
MVP-0 ships both dials with the safe positions working — autonomy full/tiered/manual, source backlog/wish — defaults autonomy=full · source=backlog. The auto work-source REFUSES with a named error until the fleet has measured its own multiplier: a strategy generator is only trustworthy once tokens-to-merged-value is a number, not a claim.
Fate questionRuling
Who advances origin/main?Autonomy dial — full by default, tiered by choice
Who authors the work?Work-source dial — backlog · wish · auto, chosen per fleet
First customer?Founder-first at FLAGSHIP grade — early users already queued; a pilot lane (manual provisioning, BYO keys) precedes billing. The bar is shows-off-Barkpark, never works-for-me

MVP-0 — setup, offload, engine

MVP-0 has three deliverables that ship as one experience: the visual setup journey (create the dev server, add a support, see the group), the first real offload (a heavy task leaves the main and the main stays fast), and the engine that makes concurrent code work safe. Zero Barkpark server changes on the engine half — fence disjointness is enforced client-side at dispatch, against the ledger that already exists.

source
Dispatch
allocator picks a fence-disjoint subset of ready tasks
→
emit
Claim
a support claims from the main's ledger — CAS; the claim IS the fence lease
→
emit
Isolate
one git worktree per cycle, never a branch switch
→
emit
Build
capacity task or bp-epic-cycle wave runs to a green local gate
→
gate
Merge-ready
signal the main — a cycle never self-merges
→
gate
Arbitrate
serial merge with a merge-base collision check, then release the fence

The three new engine components

Fence allocator
Reads ready tasks' fence labels plus currently-claimed fences, emits a disjoint subset. Client-side; no schema migration.
Merge arbiter
Lock, merge-base collision check, serial gh merge, advance main, release the fence, tell supports to pull.
Dispatcher
Routes capacity tasks and launches concurrent cycles in isolated worktrees, supervising their heartbeats.

...and the cockpit slices that ride with them

The group object
A fleet grouping anchored on the main, so the console can draw the fleet card and status, open, usage and rollout can scope to ONE group.
Add-support flow + role addressing
The one-click provision-and-bind journey in the console, and addressing members by role — main, support-2 — closing PDS gap G5.
Capacity-aware herd + one-click enter
Capacity tasks, cycles, claims, fences and the merge queue join the attention-sorted views; the tmux console becomes reachable per-support from the fleet card.

Acceptance — three proofs, one of them negative

What done means
Journey: a stranger walks create → add support → see the group, unaided, in the console. Offload: one heavy capacity task — a full workspace export of the class the main provably cannot afford — runs on a support while the main stays responsive, visibly. Engine: two fence-disjoint canary cycles run concurrently and merge serially; then two deliberately OVERLAPPING fences are injected and the allocator is PROVEN to refuse them. Without the negative half, the allocator's green proves nothing.
Out of scope for MVP-0, in writing
Groups beyond 1 main + 2 supports · the Chat-agent driver (MVP-0 uses external Claude Code) · lease-lapse and resilience automation · the auto work-source (the dial ships; that position refuses until the multiplier is measured) · and ALL of commerce. Note what is NOT deferred: the visual journey and gate hardening both ride MVP-0, because the journey is the product and full-auto is the default.

The infrastructure unit

An earlier cut of this plan recommended one box per fleet with soft-isolated members. The offload purpose kills that: a support on the main's own box adds no capacity — offload REQUIRES another box. So the ruling is amended, and it is simpler:

UnitRuling
The groupThe product, billing and cockpit unit: one main + its supports, anchored on the main
The memberEvery member is its own instance — the existing provisioning unit (site-spawner, instance lifecycle, Hetzner client). Add-support = provision + bind.
IsolationCross-customer isolation falls out for free (separate boxes). Intra-group trust is soft — same owner, same repo — over the members' private channel.
SizingSupports are sized per task class: a big-memory support for exports, lean ones for cycles. The main stays ≥16 GB; a support's size is a property of its job.
Why sized-to-task supports matter
The crown-proof export demands 2235 MiB beside a live BEAM — impossible on the 3.8 GB main it was tried on, trivial on an 8–16 GB support that runs nothing else. Capacity classes turn a structural impossibility into a dropdown choice.

Pricing

The hub-and-spoke shape makes pricing honest and incremental: the base is the $29 dev server you already have; the upsell unit is the support server. No fleet SKU, no tier table to study — you add capacity the way you add it in the console: one support at a time, priced by size class.

Sophistication lives in bounding the variable that bites. The COGS has two parts and they behave nothing alike:

Cost of goods, by volatility
Token spend
80%dominant · variable · can turn a sale into a loss
The boxes
20%fixed per support · modest · predictable
The recurring failure this must not reproduce
Concurrent cycles burn tokens fast, and this project's own record shows the monthly spend limit being hit repeatedly. Never bundle unbounded tokens into a flat price. The instruments already exist — the fleet-wide token meter is in the engine plan, and the repo carries a verified cost formula (note that cache writes are roughly 59% of agent cost).
BaseThe main Your Personal Development Server, unchanged at its rung. The fleet is an attachment to it, never a replacement for it.
UpsellPer support Each support is priced like a PDS plus an orchestration premium, by size class. Adding and removing supports is elastic — a support is disposable by doctrine, so month-to-month elasticity is honest.
TokensMetered or BYO Bring-your-own key, or metered pass-through with margin — always behind a HARD per-fleet cap that halts cycles, not just updates. The cap is a product feature, reusing the meter the main needs anyway.

The sequence

Setup + OffloadGroup + PilotsCommerce
MVP-0 · Setup + offload + engine — the console journey, one real offload, canary pair, negative fence test
 
MVP-1 · Full group + pilots — 1 main + 4 supports, cycle-halting spend cap fires, first outside users
 
MVP-2 · Commerce — self-serve provisioning, billing, per-support metering
 
StageProves
MVP-0 Setup + offload + engineA stranger walks the journey; a heavy task provably leaves the main; the fence allocator can actually refuse — all visual, all in the console
MVP-1 Full group + pilotsFour-support concurrency, the cycle-halting spend cap firing before spend runs away, and the first queued outside users running their own fleets via the pilot lane
MVP-2 CommerceA fleet grows from the console for someone who is not you — metered per support and billable

Open questions

1. Flagship group size. Is 1 main + 4 supports the shape the marketing leads with, or is capacity-by-class (one big export support + N cycle supports) the honest headline?
2. Support size classes. Uniform supports, or task-class sizing (export-class, cycle-class) from day one? Class sizing is more honest to the offload story but adds a choice to the add-support flow.
3. Token economics. BYO key or metered pass-through as the default? BYO bounds risk to near zero; metered captures more revenue but carries spend exposure.
4. Group addressing. Should the group be a first-class noun (bp fleet ...) or a label that scopes existing bp cloud verbs? The label is cheaper and keeps the design law; the noun reads better.
5. Local fleet parity. The twin doctrine says a free local fleet must be possible — how many supports does one local machine honestly sustain before the box is the limit?
Immediate next step
File the Personal Dev Fleet epic and cut the MVP-0 tasks: the group object, the add-support console flow, the dispatcher with capacity routing, the fence allocator, the merge arbiter, the offload proof, and the positive-plus-negative fence acceptance. Then the fleet starts building itself, through bp-epic-cycle — the same way it will build everything else.

See the fleetbp cloud status — every Barkpark ranked, bucketed: attention · in-flight · healthy
Watch the agentsbp chat — lands on “the herd”: agent-state pills, sorted blocked-first
Enter an instancebp cloud open instance <name> deep link · Studio tmux console, admin-gated
Auth once, reach allbp login device-link + bp instance credentials <id> — the minted admin token, no SSH
Switch contextbp use / bp servers — named, known, active
Meter spendbp cloud usage — honest counts, never a fake zero
Fleet-wide brakebp cloud rollout halt
Provision · ship · gatebp cloud instance create · bp cloud deploy · bp cloud verify
Cycle ledgerbp cycle — already one project-scoped authority for local AND cloud agents
The design law that follows Do not build a new control surface — extend the console, bp cloud and the herd. A Personal Dev Fleet that requires its own bespoke console has already failed the convenience test it exists to pass. Visual first, CLI parity always.

The five genuine gaps

Gap 1
No group object Instances are a flat list. Nothing says these ARE one group anchored on a main — so status, open, usage and rollout cannot scope to a fleet, and the console cannot draw the fleet card.
Gap 2
No fleet context bp use is per-server; there is no group context unit and no way to address a member by ROLE — main, support-2. This is PDS gap G5, still open.
Gap 3
No cycle brake bp cloud rollout halt brakes autoupdates, not WORK. A fleet-scoped spend cap that halts running cycles does not exist yet — and it is the guardrail the pricing model depends on.
Gap 4
Herd is chat-only The herd shows chat sessions with agent-state pills. A fleet operator also needs capacity tasks, cycles, claims, fences and the merge queue in that same attention-sorted view.
Gap 5
Console not fleet-reachable The Studio tmux console exists and is admin-gated by default, but is not reachable per-support FROM the fleet card — which is exactly the enter-easily path.
What this buys Closing five gaps against surfaces that already rank, open, authenticate, meter and brake is a fraction of building a fleet console from scratch — and it means the fleet is operable from the first support it ever gains.
§

The two dials

A hostile review of this plan surfaced three fate questions — who may advance main, who authors the work, who is the first customer. The answers came back with one shape: the two decisions that determine what this product IS are not policies to fix — they are fleet-level dials, surfaced in the cockpit, switchable per fleet.

Dial 1 — Autonomy
full · tiered · manual. FULL is the default: the fleet merges on green and you sample afterward. Tiered by choice: auto-merge on low-risk fences, human approval on core paths — the fence map doubles as the trust map. Manual caps throughput at your attention.
Dial 2 — Work source
backlog · wish · auto. Backlog drains the existing ready-task pool. Wish: you write high-level wishes and the main runs strategize-then-decide to cut and fence the roster. Auto: the fleet generates its own strategy — the biggest agent risk, sequenced last.
Full-auto by default makes the gate the safety case If the default is merge-on-green with no human in the loop, the green must be one a broken build could NOT also produce. Gate hardening stops being hygiene and becomes the product's core safety property: protective tests, mutation-proven guards, and an arbiter that refuses advisory-red merges. This joins MVP-0's acceptance, not its backlog.
The dials land in order MVP-0 ships both dials with the safe positions working — autonomy full/tiered/manual, source backlog/wish — defaults autonomy=full · source=backlog. The auto work-source REFUSES with a named error until the fleet has measured its own multiplier: a strategy generator is only trustworthy once tokens-to-merged-value is a number, not a claim.
Fate questionRuling
Who advances origin/main?Autonomy dial — full by default, tiered by choice
Who authors the work?Work-source dial — backlog · wish · auto, chosen per fleet
First customer?Founder-first at FLAGSHIP grade — early users already queued; a pilot lane (manual provisioning, BYO keys) precedes billing. The bar is shows-off-Barkpark, never works-for-me
§

MVP-0 — setup, offload, engine

MVP-0 has three deliverables that ship as one experience: the visual setup journey (create the dev server, add a support, see the group), the first real offload (a heavy task leaves the main and the main stays fast), and the engine that makes concurrent code work safe. Zero Barkpark server changes on the engine half — fence disjointness is enforced client-side at dispatch, against the ledger that already exists.

The three new engine components

Fence allocator
Reads ready tasks' fence labels plus currently-claimed fences, emits a disjoint subset. Client-side; no schema migration.
Merge arbiter
Lock, merge-base collision check, serial gh merge, advance main, release the fence, tell supports to pull.
Dispatcher
Routes capacity tasks and launches concurrent cycles in isolated worktrees, supervising their heartbeats.

...and the cockpit slices that ride with them

The group object
A fleet grouping anchored on the main, so the console can draw the fleet card and status, open, usage and rollout can scope to ONE group.
Add-support flow + role addressing
The one-click provision-and-bind journey in the console, and addressing members by role — main, support-2 — closing PDS gap G5.
Capacity-aware herd + one-click enter
Capacity tasks, cycles, claims, fences and the merge queue join the attention-sorted views; the tmux console becomes reachable per-support from the fleet card.

Acceptance — three proofs, one of them negative

What done means Journey: a stranger walks create → add support → see the group, unaided, in the console. Offload: one heavy capacity task — a full workspace export of the class the main provably cannot afford — runs on a support while the main stays responsive, visibly. Engine: two fence-disjoint canary cycles run concurrently and merge serially; then two deliberately OVERLAPPING fences are injected and the allocator is PROVEN to refuse them. Without the negative half, the allocator's green proves nothing.
Out of scope for MVP-0, in writing Groups beyond 1 main + 2 supports · the Chat-agent driver (MVP-0 uses external Claude Code) · lease-lapse and resilience automation · the auto work-source (the dial ships; that position refuses until the multiplier is measured) · and ALL of commerce. Note what is NOT deferred: the visual journey and gate hardening both ride MVP-0, because the journey is the product and full-auto is the default.
§

The infrastructure unit

An earlier cut of this plan recommended one box per fleet with soft-isolated members. The offload purpose kills that: a support on the main's own box adds no capacity — offload REQUIRES another box. So the ruling is amended, and it is simpler:

UnitRuling
The groupThe product, billing and cockpit unit: one main + its supports, anchored on the main
The memberEvery member is its own instance — the existing provisioning unit (site-spawner, instance lifecycle, Hetzner client). Add-support = provision + bind.
IsolationCross-customer isolation falls out for free (separate boxes). Intra-group trust is soft — same owner, same repo — over the members' private channel.
SizingSupports are sized per task class: a big-memory support for exports, lean ones for cycles. The main stays ≥16 GB; a support's size is a property of its job.
Why sized-to-task supports matter The crown-proof export demands 2235 MiB beside a live BEAM — impossible on the 3.8 GB main it was tried on, trivial on an 8–16 GB support that runs nothing else. Capacity classes turn a structural impossibility into a dropdown choice.
§

Pricing

The hub-and-spoke shape makes pricing honest and incremental: the base is the $29 dev server you already have; the upsell unit is the support server. No fleet SKU, no tier table to study — you add capacity the way you add it in the console: one support at a time, priced by size class.

Sophistication lives in bounding the variable that bites. The COGS has two parts and they behave nothing alike:

Cost of goods, by volatility
Token spend80%dominant · variable · can turn a sale into a loss
The boxes20%fixed per support · modest · predictable
The recurring failure this must not reproduce Concurrent cycles burn tokens fast, and this project's own record shows the monthly spend limit being hit repeatedly. Never bundle unbounded tokens into a flat price. The instruments already exist — the fleet-wide token meter is in the engine plan, and the repo carries a verified cost formula (note that cache writes are roughly 59% of agent cost).
Base
The main Your Personal Development Server, unchanged at its rung. The fleet is an attachment to it, never a replacement for it.
Upsell
Per support Each support is priced like a PDS plus an orchestration premium, by size class. Adding and removing supports is elastic — a support is disposable by doctrine, so month-to-month elasticity is honest.
Tokens
Metered or BYO Bring-your-own key, or metered pass-through with margin — always behind a HARD per-fleet cap that halts cycles, not just updates. The cap is a product feature, reusing the meter the main needs anyway.
§

The sequence

Setup + OffloadGroup + PilotsCommerce
MVP-0 · Setup + offload + engine — the console journey, one real offload, canary pair, negative fence test
MVP-1 · Full group + pilots — 1 main + 4 supports, cycle-halting spend cap fires, first outside users
MVP-2 · Commerce — self-serve provisioning, billing, per-support metering
StageProves
MVP-0 Setup + offload + engineA stranger walks the journey; a heavy task provably leaves the main; the fence allocator can actually refuse — all visual, all in the console
MVP-1 Full group + pilotsFour-support concurrency, the cycle-halting spend cap firing before spend runs away, and the first queued outside users running their own fleets via the pilot lane
MVP-2 CommerceA fleet grows from the console for someone who is not you — metered per support and billable
§

Open questions

  1. Flagship group size. Is 1 main + 4 supports the shape the marketing leads with, or is capacity-by-class (one big export support + N cycle supports) the honest headline?
  2. Support size classes. Uniform supports, or task-class sizing (export-class, cycle-class) from day one? Class sizing is more honest to the offload story but adds a choice to the add-support flow.
  3. Token economics. BYO key or metered pass-through as the default? BYO bounds risk to near zero; metered captures more revenue but carries spend exposure.
  4. Group addressing. Should the group be a first-class noun (bp fleet ...) or a label that scopes existing bp cloud verbs? The label is cheaper and keeps the design law; the noun reads better.
  5. Local fleet parity. The twin doctrine says a free local fleet must be possible — how many supports does one local machine honestly sustain before the box is the limit?
Immediate next step File the Personal Dev Fleet epic and cut the MVP-0 tasks: the group object, the add-support console flow, the dispatcher with capacity routing, the fence allocator, the merge arbiter, the offload proof, and the positive-plus-negative fence acceptance. Then the fleet starts building itself, through bp-epic-cycle — the same way it will build everything else.

tags.rationale: Personal Dev Fleet is the product being planned; the group anchored on the main is the billing and cockpit unit.
The main IS a Personal Development Server and every support provisions through the PDS data plane.
The visual setup journey lives in the Barkpark Cloud console and reuses its provisioning and lifecycle machinery.
Support servers are the capacity workers; per-support pricing and sizing classes are the product levers.
